# Claude Code Tray

> A native Windows (10/11) system-tray monitor for Claude Code usage. It shows your
> rate-limit usage percentage as a crisp, DPI-aware vector icon, projects when you'll
> hit 100% (a pace line for the weekly window, burn-rate regression for the 5h session),
> and provides a privacy-first 24h usage breakdown computed locally. Built in C# (.NET 10,
> WinForms + GDI+). Zero configuration — it reuses the OAuth token Claude Code already
> stores on your machine. Installable via the Windows Package Manager:
> `winget install alegauss.ClaudeCodeTray`.

This is an unofficial, open-source community project (Apache License 2.0). It is not
affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Anthropic. "Claude" and "Claude Code" are
trademarks of Anthropic; the tool only reads usage data Claude Code already exposes locally.

## Features

- **Crisp at any DPI**: the percentage is drawn as a vector at the exact tray size (no downscaled bitmaps), sharp on 125–200% displays.
- **Task-Manager-style fill bar**: a vertical bar rises with usage; blue when on track, vivid red when projected to exhaust before the window resets.
- **Smart projection**: warns before the window resets, not after. The weekly (7d) window uses a proportional pace line (usage vs. the share an even burn would have spent by now), accurate from the first reading; the 5h session and extra windows use least-squares regression over a short rolling history of utilization samples.
- **Activity-aware weekly pacing**: the Statistics window's weekly projection is spent along the hours you are actually active — a 168-bucket day-of-week x hour profile mined from the timestamps in your local transcripts — instead of uniformly across the clock. It stays flat through the stretches you are usually idle (shaded faintly on the chart) and climbs through your working hours, so the exhaustion marker lands at a plausible time rather than at 4 a.m. Needs about three weeks of local transcripts; below that it falls back to the straight average-pace line. The even-pace line, the verdict chip and the tray icon stay wall-clock. When it projects running out early it also names the earliest hour you normally work that you could resume at and still finish the week under the limit ("stop now and pick it back up around Thursday 13:00, and you'd close the week at about 97%"), or says nothing if no such hour exists. Last week's burn-up is drawn faintly behind the current one on the same axes once two weeks of history exist, answering "is this week worse than the last?" without a second chart or a new number. CLI: `--activity` prints the measured week as a heatmap.
- **Live throughput**: under each Statistics chart, a second number on a second clock. The window average answers "what did this window cost"; below it, "Now ~ N tok/s" answers "what is running now". The moving picture behind that number has its own third tab, **Throughput**: two line charts of the last three minutes - one line per project above, one per token type below, both always drawn - with both window averages beneath them for scale. It lives on its own tab because it is the only thing in the window with no window scope, so "now" was otherwise the same picture on both pace tabs. Read from the local transcripts as they are appended - a byte-level tail with a filesystem watcher, no extra API calls and no change to the rate-limit polling cadence. What the lines plot is the rolling rate (the same age-weighted 60s kernel as the number above them, sampled once a second, attack-smoothed the same way), not the raw per-second counts: a turn's tokens are recorded in the second it finished, so the raw buckets are events, and joining events with a line would draw a rate that never existed. A rolling rate is continuous - it slides down through a pause because the work really is ageing out of the window and climbs when new work lands - and its right-hand end equals the number printed above. Neither chart is a mode: an earlier single chart switched from the by-type view to the by-project view when a second repo started generating, which changed what its colours meant mid-read. Each project keeps a fixed colour and legend position for as long as it has anything on screen, and a repo that goes quiet decays toward zero and ages off the left edge instead of vanishing. Height is a quantity: each chart's ceiling is ruled and labelled in tok/s at the right edge with its half on a dashed line, taken from the highest point visible rounded up to a readable step - or, when the peak is more than 2x the 95th percentile of the moving samples, the percentile instead, with the runs above it drawn dashed along the ceiling rather than silently truncated. One line under both charts reports the cache re-read rate and its ratio to the work above it (measured here: ~30,000 tok/s of cache read against ~150 tok/s of real work, a ~200x ratio). Cache reads are excluded from every rate on the tab because they barely weigh on the rate limit, and that exclusion is stated where it is made: the number is the user's context being re-sent with every turn, which makes it the per-turn price of a large eager context and the link to the Context Load Inspector, which measures that context statically. The ratio is dropped when the work rate is too low to divide by. Pointing at a chart reads one second out of it: a crosshair snaps to the nearest second, a dot marks each line, and a readout names the time, every series' rate through that second and the tokens that actually landed in it - two different quantities on purpose, since the rate is a trailing minute, so a second that carried nothing can still sit high on the line (earlier work ageing out, which the reading says). The readout is drawn inside the plot rather than as a tooltip, and it states what full height means, how many samples ran past it and what the real peak was whenever anything is being clipped. The axis is dropped while a chart is flat. Both numbers are token throughput, not quota, and an empty chart means no turn landed on this machine (work on another machine or on claude.ai leaves no transcript here). The row also reports how many sessions are active (a session counts as active on a turn in the last two minutes, not on file presence); the heaviest four repos get a line and the rest fold into one grey "others". CLI: `--live` prints the rate, the active-session count, the per-project split with each project's slot and every series as a sparkline; `--tail` prints turns as they land.
- **Color-coded reset notifications**: when a usage window hands quota back, a bespoke on-brand toast (confetti + a refilling quota bar) appears, with a distinct color/headline per kind — clay "Surprise!" (early weekly reset), violet "Bonus!" (mid-window credit), teal "New week!" (routine weekly reset), blue "Fresh session!" (5h session reset). All on by default; each toggles independently in Settings.
- **24h usage insights**: local, cost-weighted breakdown by model, subagents, and large-context requests — read only from session transcripts, never message content.
- **Context load inspector**: shows what every session in a project loads *before the first prompt* — the instruction chain, the memory index and every skill/agent description — as a session-zero gauge against the 200k window, with Claude Code's own ~32k system-prompt overhead as its own segment and the transcript-measured startup context overlaid. Splits eager (paid every request) from lazy (paid only when used), annotates each skill "45x" or "never" from real invocations, grades each project A-F, tracks weekly drift, and reports grounded findings (oversized memory index, dead index pointers, memory directories duplicated between worktrees, dead project directories, oversized skill descriptions) each with a concrete fix. Read-only: the single action is copying a cleanup prompt for Claude Code. CLI: `--context`, `--context --check`, `--context --usage`, `--context-report <file.md>`.
- **System information page**: a read-only Settings page that answers "which plan is this login on, and what is this install?" without opening a JSON file. Names the plan the way a person says it (the `userRateLimitTier` behind it mapped to e.g. "Claude Max 5x", with the raw tier, seat tier and billing type as its qualifier, and an unrecognized tier shown verbatim rather than hidden), plus whether extra usage is enabled, when this login first spent a token through Claude Code, and how long the stored sign-in is valid. Then the install: CLI version (the newest in the native installer's version store), install method, auto-update state, how many projects Claude Code tracks, and the configuration folder with a button to open it (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` honoured). Then the machine: the tray's version and location, the Windows build, the .NET runtime and the architecture. The account holder, the email and every absolute path are **masked by default** (initials, `a•••••@example.com`, paths folded back to `~`) because this is the page that ends up in a screenshot attached to a bug report; one button reveals them and hides them again, and "Copy for a bug report" copies the page as plain text exactly as displayed, so a masked holder stays masked. Every reading comes from files Claude Code already keeps locally (`.claude.json`, `.claude/.credentials.json`) — no API call, nothing written, no transcript read, and no secret displayed: the credentials file is read only for its expiry, subscription type and the number of granted permissions.
- **Several Claude Code profiles on one machine**: Claude Code stores one account per configuration directory (`.claude.json` holds a single `oauthAccount`, `/login` overwrites it), so several subscriptions on one Windows means several config dirs via `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. The tray discovers every one of them — the dir it would itself use, `~/.claude`, an `env.CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` in either one's `settings.json`, the same key in each registered project's `.claude/settings.json`/`settings.local.json`, and the `~/.claude-*` naming convention — and the System information page offers a picker that re-reads the whole page from the chosen profile's own files. Identity is the account uuid, so the same account reached through two paths is listed once; labels are derived (organization name, else "Personal", else the folder name) and never typed. With a single profile, which is the normal case, the picker is hidden entirely. Read-only: discovery opens files and never writes one. CLI: `--profiles [dir...]`.
- **Switching profiles from the tray**: Settings → Claude Code → Profiles keeps a list of `{name, configuration folder, working directory}` — and nothing else: no address, no token, no plan, so the tray never becomes a second store of credentials. Renaming is a text box; typing a name into an automatically discovered profile is what registers it. Removing takes it out of the tray's list only — the folder, its login, its transcripts and its memory are never touched, and a still-discoverable folder returns as a found profile. With more than one profile, the tray's **Open Claude Code** becomes a submenu: each entry launches Claude Code with that profile's `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and its own working directory, so one click cannot open a work account inside a personal repo. It collapses back to a single command while **Use the chosen profile everywhere in Windows** is on, because the environment already carries the picked profile and every entry would open the same session — the sign-in marking survives the collapse (T146). By default the variable is set on the launched process only, so a terminal the user opens themselves still gets the default profile; that opt-in toggle is the one place the tray writes a user-scope variable, and switching it off puts the previous value back (T145). It is **not** set at all for the default profile: that dir is what a bare `claude` already uses, and overriding it to the same path makes Claude Code run against a near-empty `~/.claude/.claude.json` with none of the user's project history, then leaves that stub behind to misdescribe the profile (fixed in T136, together with the reader that had started believing the stub over the real `~/.claude.json`). A profile with no credentials file is marked and its entry runs `claude auth login`, with `--email` prefilled only when the folder's config already names the account whose login lapsed; the profiles are re-discovered every time the menu opens (5–6ms with two profiles), so a profile that has just signed in stops being offered a sign-in instead of sending the user to the browser a second time (T137). Nothing is ever written into a configuration folder — Claude Code creates a missing one itself and owns every file in it — and credentials are never copied or swapped between folders, which is what makes this safe: Claude Code rewrites its own credentials file on each token refresh (an 8-hour access token, a 5-day refresh token), so file-shuffling races that refresher and costs the user a login. A running session keeps the profile it started with; a change applies to the next one. With more than one profile the icon also carries a per-profile identity band along its top edge (T147): the number, the fill and the projection colour are identical whichever profile the icon follows, so nothing else on the tile answers "whose number is this?". It is a colour band rather than the profile's initial because at the real 16px a second glyph and the number cannot both be read — measured, not assumed — and the number is what the app exists to show; the band lands inside the margin already left above the digits and costs them nothing. Its hues (violet, pink, periwinkle) are disjoint from every colour that already carries meaning (the green/orange/red projection, the cyan "no projection yet", the amber API error, the slate tile), so identity and verdict share neither a hue nor a form — the verdict is a level rising from the bottom, identity is a fixed band at the top. The slot is the profile's position in the watch list ordered by key, not the list's own order, since the followed profile is always first and indexing that would give every profile the same band the moment it took the icon over. CLI: `--profiles` prints each profile's menu label, resolved command, config dir, working directory and the accent band it wears.
- **Which credentials a profile actually uses (and whether the percentages describe it)**: `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` isolates files but not environment authentication. On a machine with an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set, a configuration folder with no completed OAuth login authenticates with that key — work there is billed per use and never touches the 5-hour or weekly windows, while the tray reads the OAuth token and draws a near-idle subscription. The System information page therefore reports each profile's effective auth (Claude subscription / API key / Amazon Bedrock / Google Vertex / not signed in), where it came from, and whether that was inferred locally or confirmed by Claude Code — with an accent-bordered warning, when the profile is off-subscription, stating that the plan, the percentages and the tray icon do not describe what Claude Code is spending there. Precedence follows the tool's own, measured: a completed OAuth login in the folder wins, otherwise an environment key takes over; env vars, the folder's `settings.json` `env` block and `apiKeyHelper` are all considered, and only the *presence* of a key is ever read — never its value. A **Check** button asks `claude auth status --json` for the authoritative answer, off the UI thread, and leaves the inferred reading in place if the call fails. CLI: `--profiles --check`.
- **Watching several profiles at once**: every registered profile is polled once per refresh interval, each with its own OAuth token and each appended to its own stored series, so a profile the icon is not showing still accumulates the history it would need if it became the monitored one. A profile that is not on the subscription is deliberately not polled — an API key has no quota window to read and the call would cost money for nothing. The tray icon shows one profile (`MonitoredConfigDir`, defaulting to the config dir a bare `claude` uses); switching clears the burn history first, because a slope fitted across two accounts' readings projects about neither and reads the jump between them as a phantom reset. The other profiles' readings live in a **Profile** submenu — one entry each with its current usage, a checkmark on the monitored one, and its own failure named ("sign-in needed") rather than a generic prompt that would send somebody to re-login on the wrong account — because the Windows tray tooltip is capped at 127 characters and cannot hold a second account; the tooltip only names which profile it is describing. The Settings cost estimate multiplies by the number of polled profiles and says so. CLI: `--profiles` also prints which profile the icon follows and how many are polled.
- **The icon follows the profile you are working in**: with more than one profile, **Follow the active profile** (in the tray's Profile submenu, and in Settings → Claude Code → Profiles; off by default) points the icon at whichever profile Claude Code last had a turn in, so switching accounts needs no click. The evidence is the newest `projects\**\*.jsonl` write timestamp under each configuration folder — directory entries only, no transcript is opened and no content is read — probed on the usage poll's own cadence rather than by a resident watcher, which is what keeps the dropped tray-animation cost (a transcript tail running all session) out of the tray. Measured at ~20ms per configuration folder over ~600 transcripts. A profile is only followed into if the icon could say something about it: it must draw on the subscription and have credentials on disk. Only a turn inside the last 30 minutes counts, and a timestamp more than two minutes in the future is ignored as a copied file or a skewed clock rather than believed. Choosing a profile by hand wins until a turn lands elsewhere *after* the click, so auto-follow never overrules the user; the submenu also shows how long ago each profile was active. CLI: `--profiles` prints each profile's last turn, which of them are candidates, and where the icon would move to.
- **Statistics per profile**: the Statistics window reports on one profile at a time and names it; with more than one profile a picker at the top switches it, and the pace charts, the projection, the activity shape, the previous-week ghost and the live throughput are all recomputed from that profile's own stored readings and its own transcripts (the transcript tail is pointed at that configuration folder, not the default one). A profile the icon is not following is drawn from its last stored reading, with the footer timestamp saying when that was; a profile with nothing stored yet says so rather than borrowing another account's numbers, and a reading pushed by the tray's poll is refused while a non-monitored profile is on screen. CLI: `--capture-stats <base> [shape] profile=<n>`.
- **Auth recovery**: on an expired token (HTTP 401) the tooltip shows a clear "not authenticated" prompt and an "Open Claude Code" menu item re-authenticates in one click.
- **Self-updating**: checks GitHub Releases and offers a one-click in-app update; per-user install, no admin rights.

## Installation

- **winget (recommended)**: `winget install alegauss.ClaudeCodeTray` — published to the Microsoft winget-pkgs community repository, with `en-US` and `pt-BR` manifest locales.
- **Direct download**: run `ClaudeTray-Setup.exe` from the latest GitHub release. Per-user install (no admin); existing installs self-update from GitHub Releases.
- **Prerequisite**: Claude Code installed and logged in at least once (`claude`), so the OAuth token exists at `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\.credentials.json`.

## Data source

- Rate-limit data: one minimal Anthropic API call (Haiku, 1 token) every 5 minutes reads the `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-*` response headers, using the OAuth token at `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\.credentials.json`.
- Usage insights: read locally from Claude Code session transcripts at `~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl` — no API call.

content tools for organisations with a lot to publish — run on your own
servers, with no per-user licence.

- **Viglet Turing ES** (https://turing.viglet.org) — Search for sites with a
  lot of content. People ask in their own words — “evening management course”,
  “engineering at the north campus” — and find it, with filters that match how
  they actually choose. AI answers using only your own published content, so
  it never invents a price or a deadline. Runs on your servers, your data
  stays in house, and there is no per-user licence.
- **Viglet Shio CMS** (https://shio.viglet.org) — A content system that takes
  the page out of the development queue: AI builds it, your communications
  team reviews and approves it, seeing exactly how it will look before it goes
  live. Every version is kept, so you can see what changed and roll back. Runs
  on your servers, no per-user licence.
- **Viglet Dumont** (https://www.viglet.org) — The same item of information
  usually lives in several places at once — a portal, a back-office system, a
  PDF, an old departmental site. This gathers it automatically from all of
  them and feeds it to the search, with nobody copying, pasting or keeping a
  spreadsheet up to date.

- [Site manifest](https://alegauss.github.io/claude-tray/manifest.json): every page of this
  site with its URL, title and the plain-Markdown twin beside it. Each page is served twice —
  `index.html` for a browser and `index.md` for a reader that does not want the markup — so
  appending `index.md` to any URL below returns the same page as text.
- [The projection](https://alegauss.github.io/claude-tray/features/projection/): the two
  forecasting models, and the four states the icon can be in

  charts, the live throughput strip, and the per-session cost at API list prices
- [The notifications](https://alegauss.github.io/claude-tray/features/notifications/): the
  four reset toasts and the three that state a fact instead of celebrating one
- [The context audit](https://alegauss.github.io/claude-tray/features/context/): what every
  session loads before the first prompt, and why it is measured and never edited
- [Privacy](https://alegauss.github.io/claude-tray/features/privacy/): what is read, what is
  not, and the one call that leaves the machine
